12. The decisive experiment to perform before building the factory

The first experiment should contain two real chemical extensions and two instruction clips.

It should test the most consequential failure: one legitimate product key advancing an illegitimate neighboring chain.

Construction and controls

Use attainable A/B peptoid chemistry first, with purified donor–key conjugates, custom two-clip supports and a 1 mL glass/PEEK flow cell.

Mix distinguishable support populations in a 1:9 ratio:

One population can form the authenticated first extension.
The other receives a hydrolyzed or nonreactive first packet while retaining its free terminal amine.

Execute coupling, duplex stripping, absorbing clearance, key exposure, nickase action, quenching, deprotection and a second feed.

Include:

No-amine and no-activator blanks.
Wrong-code packets.
Deliberately retained noncovalent packets.
An authenticated wrong covalent extension.
Missing donor.
Incomplete enzyme quenching.
Three independent stock preparations.
At least three repeated couple–clear–advance–reset cycles.

Do not infer it by multiplying separate average fluorescence and average chemical-yield measurements.

Separate cut and uncut register fractions, or use distinguishable stable-isotope initiators, and chemically analyse their products. Fluorescence can report clip state; LC–MS/MS and precursor NMR establish chemistry.

Meter total electricity, flow, pressure, temperature, irradiation, wash effluent, retained material and reagent inputs.

Numerical primitive criteria
At least 99.5% correct clip transition under the specified gating interval.
At most 0.1% false advancement per failed scaffold.
No more than one newly opened instruction per authenticated extension.
At most 0.5% chemical loss during clearance/reset.
No second-monomer incorporation without the first above the validated threshold.
Regenerated terminal chemistry capable of the next actual coupling.
